The deck team will be standing by fore and aft from thirty minutes before the pilot boards.
The arrangements will have been verified by name and not by signature.
By the end of the quarter the company will have replaced every emergency signal card in the fleet.
The fire was contained by the fixed fire suppression system within four minutes.
The order to abandon ship was never given, and no distress call was transmitted.

The fixed system did exactly what it was designed to do, and I want that on the record, because everything else I am going to say sounds like criticism. Four minutes from detection to containment, compartment sealed, no distress call, nobody hurt. If you read only the numbers it is a good day. What the numbers do not show is that two people arrived at the wrong muster station and asked me where they should be, and that when I went to check the forward locker afterwards I could not open it, because somebody had painted it shut at the last dry dock and nobody had opened it since. We were four minutes and a closed door away from a very different conversation. The order to abandon ship was never given. That is the only reason those two things are anecdotes and not findings.

I will tell you what this instruction does and what it does not do, because I would rather say it than have it discovered. It does not make anybody safer on its own. Nothing written down does. What it changes is one word: verification is by name, not by signature. From the first of next month, by the time a ship reaches the pilot station her crew will have completed the round person by person, and the master will be reporting it that way, out loud, on the record. By the end of the quarter we will have replaced every emergency signal card in the fleet, which will take four months and cost less than one day of detention. And the honest measure of whether any of it worked is not the paperwork. It is whether the next two people who go to the wrong station are doing it in a drill.
